name: Declan Fitzgerald
presenting_complaint: Ongoing generalised tonic-clonic seizure, still convulsing on arrival

medications: Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily (recently non-adherent)
medical_history.social: Lives alone. Heavy alcohol intake, last drink 2 days ago. Ran out of valproate 4 days ago.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 34-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that started at least 12 minutes ago (paramedics gave IM midazolam 10 mg en route with no effect) and he is still convulsing on arrival. Known epilepsy, recently non-adherent to valproate, and 2 days since his last alcohol. He is cyanosed around the lips. Obs: BP 156/94, HR 128, RR 22, SpO2 90% on 15 L, GCS 6, and a bedside BGL of 2.9 mmol/L.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Seizure timeline: continuous convulsion >5 min (established status epilepticus by definition), onset time and prehospital midazolam 10 mg IM already given without response
Known epilepsy with recent valproate non-adherence (missed 4 days) as likely precipitant
Screen precipitants: alcohol withdrawal (last drink 2 days ago), missed antiepileptics, infection/meningism, head injury, illicit drugs, pregnancy (N/A - male)
Collateral history from paramedics/family: total seizure duration, prior status, current medications and doses
Document allergies and last oral intake / aspiration risk
objective: Immediate bedside capillary BGL — documented 2.9 mmol/L (hypoglycaemia is a treatable cause and must be corrected)
ABC assessment: airway patency with jaw thrust + oropharyngeal adjunct, high-flow oxygen 15 L via non-rebreather, suction, SpO2 90% documented
Neurological exam between/after seizure: GCS 6, pupils, focal deficit, signs of head trauma, meningism, tongue biting, incontinence
Continuous cardiac + SpO2 monitoring, temperature (rule out febrile/sepsis), and end-tidal CO2 if available
IV access x2 with bloods drawn: BGL, UEC, calcium/magnesium, FBC, LFTs, antiepileptic drug levels (valproate), venous gas, ethanol/toxicology, beta-hCG N/A
assessment: Established generalised convulsive status epilepticus (>5 minutes continuous seizure, refractory to first benzodiazepine)
Precipitant likely antiepileptic non-adherence and/or alcohol withdrawal; hypoglycaemia (BGL 2.9) contributing and must be corrected
Consider and exclude: CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis), intracranial haemorrhage/mass, metabolic derangement (Na, Ca, Mg), toxic ingestion
Impending airway compromise / hypoxia (SpO2 90%, GCS 6) — anticipate need for definitive airway if seizure continues
plan: Correct hypoglycaemia immediately: 100 mL of 10% glucose IV (or 50 mL 50% dextrose) plus thiamine 300 mg IV (before/with glucose in alcohol dependence) for Wernicke prevention
Give a benzodiazepine now and START THE CLOCK: IV lorazepam 4 mg (or IV diazepam 10 mg); as prehospital IM midazolam 10 mg already given, this is the second/definitive benzodiazepine dose

If still seizing 5 minutes after the benzodiazepine, ESCALATE to second-line IV antiepileptic: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g) IV, OR sodium valproate 40 mg/kg IV, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV at max 50 mg/min with cardiac monitoring
Do NOT simply repeat further benzodiazepines instead of escalating — move up the ladder by the clock
Airway/breathing support: high-flow O2, suction, airway adjunct; call anaesthetics/ICU early for rapid sequence intubation if refractory (seizing beyond second-line)

Investigate cause: UEC, calcium, magnesium, FBC, LFTs, valproate level, venous gas, toxicology; treat/replace derangements; CT brain and consider LP once seizure controlled and safe; treat suspected CNS infection empirically (e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g IV + aciclovir) if meningoencephalitis suspected
Treat alcohol withdrawal contribution with benzodiazepines and ongoing thiamine; admit to HDU/ICU with neurology involvement
Continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring, reassess GCS and re-check BGL after glucose

critical_errors: Repeatedly giving benzodiazepine after benzodiazepine instead of escalating up the ladder to a second-line IV antiepileptic (levetiracetam/valproate/phenytoin) when seizing continues
Failing to check and correct the bedside BGL — missing hypoglycaemia (2.9 mmol/L) as a treatable cause of the ongoing seizure
Under-dosing the benzodiazepine (giving a sub-therapeutic dose and not delivering the full weight-appropriate benzodiazepine/second-line dose)
must_not_miss: Hypoglycaemia as the seizure cause — check and correct BGL immediately
Ongoing seizure activity requiring escalation to a second-line IV antiepileptic and early anaesthetics/ICU for a definitive airway
CNS infection or intracranial catastrophe considered once the seizure is controlled
